zone: Wolframite Mountain — the Tungsten Creek trail and the Boundary Trail
_areas_note: READ THIS BEFORE ADDING ANY OTHER PEAK TO THIS FILE, AND READ IT BEFORE ASSUMING WOLFRAMITE NEEDS ONE. Wolframite Mountain is an 8,137 ft summit in the far north-east Pasayten, and the Boundary Trail crosses its southern flank at the junction with the Tungsten Creek trail at about 6,750 ft — which is the site of the TUNGSTEN MINE CAMP. That camp is ALREADY WRITTEN UP in the Cathedral file, where it is recorded as sitting on the loop leg between Apex Pass and the Chewuch drainage. It is not near Wolframite; it is on Wolframite, half a mile east of the old mine workings on the peak's own south side. So the honest finding is that this peak IS genuinely served by an existing camp, and its id would sit perfectly well in the Cathedral file beside Cathedral Peak and Amphitheater Mountain, all three of which are climbed off the same stretch of Boundary Trail on the same trip. This file exists because the Tungsten Creek approach corridor itself, the Boundary Trail camps east of the junction and the ground around Apex Pass are described by nothing, and a party coming up the Chewuch for Wolframite alone sleeps in all three before it ever reaches the mine. TUNGSTEN MINE CAMP IS DELIBERATELY NOT REPEATED BELOW. Neither is anything from the eastern Pasayten file — Four Point Lake, the lower Chewuch River camps out of Thirtymile, Horseshoe Basin with Sunny Pass and Louden Lake, the Middle Fork river camps, the Shellrock bench and Dot Lake are all written there and none appears here. THE APPROACH. The normal line is the Thirtymile trailhead out of Winthrop, up the Chewuch River trail for roughly eight miles, then the Tungsten Creek trail climbing beside its creek for about six miles to the Boundary Trail junction on the peak's south side. The Cathedral Driveway trail is the alternative start, longer to drive to. From the junction the Boundary Trail runs about a mile west to where it bends south toward Apex Pass, and the summit is taken off-trail north-east up the gentle west side — mostly easy scrambling, with harder variations if the line is picked badly. From the east, the Boundary Trail continues roughly fourteen miles to Horseshoe Basin and the Iron Gate trailhead. THE 2026 CLOSURE PICTURE IS SEVERE AND MUST BE CHECKED FIRST. The Sinlahekin Fire, over 150,000 acres by mid-August 2026, closed the Iron Gate, Chewuch, Fourteen Mile and Chopaka trailheads and several campgrounds through the end of October, which is both ends of this route; the Chewuch corridor out of Thirtymile was reported as the piece most likely to stay passable and was being cleared by volunteers, but that is not the same as open. Confirm before planning.

sites.name: The Tungsten Creek trail camps below the Boundary Trail junction
sites.capacity: Scattered informal sites along the climb beside the creek, most taking one or two tents, with the better ground in the lower half where the timber is still standing. Nothing developed and no facilities, and you are unlikely to meet anyone.
sites.water: Tungsten Creek runs alongside for the whole climb and is the dependable supply on this approach, holding into the autumn. THIS IS WHERE YOU FILL FOR THE SUMMIT, because the Boundary Trail crest above the junction runs on tarns and snowmelt and is unreliable by August, and the peak itself carries nothing. Old iron pipe from the mining days is scattered along the trail, which tells you where the workings took their water and not that any of it is usable now. Treat everything.
sites.permit: Pasayten Wilderness, national forest ground, and the permit expectation is the easy one: a FREE self-issued permit filled out at the trailhead kiosk, no quota, no reservation and nothing to arrange in advance. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is needed to park at Thirtymile. Stock parties need certified weed-free feed and may not tie animals to trees overnight — this is heavily used horse country. Campfires are legal in existing rings outside a burn ban, but bans run most of the summer in this dry drainage and the wood is scarce enough that most parties do without.
sites.notes: This is where a party climbing Wolframite from the Chewuch actually sleeps on the second night, and it matters because the arithmetic of the approach is punishing without it. The Tungsten Creek trail breaks off the Chewuch trail a little past eight miles and climbs steadily for about six more, with the creek on the left and the bulk of Wolframite ahead — so a party that has walked in from Thirtymile is looking at a long day before the climbing even begins. Breaking the climb here rather than pushing to the Boundary Trail junction puts you on running water, in shelter, and with the steep work done in the cool of the morning. It is also the sensible fallback when the ground at the junction is occupied by a horse party, which happens more often than the remoteness suggests. Expect burned forest in stretches, little shade, and blowdown that changes with every windstorm. Late July through September is the working season; snow holds on the north sides of the passes above into July.

sites.name: The Boundary Trail horse camp east of the Tungsten junction
sites.capacity: An established site roughly a mile east of the junction with the Tungsten Creek trail, laid out with horse feed in mind, so it takes a stock party comfortably and a walking party easily. One of very few genuinely prepared camps along this stretch of the Boundary Trail.
sites.water: Seasonal and worth checking rather than assuming. There is water at the site early in the year and it becomes unreliable as the summer goes on, in common with everything on this crest — parties have found streams dry and pools with cracked bottoms along this trail in September. Carry up from Tungsten Creek if you are arriving late in the season.
sites.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit from the trailhead kiosk, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Weed-free feed for stock and no tying animals to trees overnight. Camp on the existing bare ground. Fires legal in existing rings outside a ban, and bans are the norm here by midsummer.
sites.notes: The obvious camp for a party climbing Wolframite and then continuing east along the Boundary Trail toward Bauerman Ridge, Teapot Dome and Horseshoe Basin, which is the classic way to use this corridor — the summits along it are all short detours off the trail with very little gain, and Wolframite is the first of them. Being a mile east of the junction it sits below the peak's south-east side rather than directly under the west approach, so a party going in and straight back out is better served staying at the mine junction ground or lower on Tungsten Creek. Its real value is that it is prepared, level and used, on a crest where most of the camping is improvised. THE WEST SIDE IS THE ROUTE. From the junction the Boundary Trail is followed roughly a mile west to where it turns south for Apex Pass, and the peak is climbed off-trail to the north-east up gentle open slopes; taken well this is easy scrambling, and taken badly it puts you on short steps of harder rock for no reason. Pick the line from below in good light rather than committing to the first gully you meet.

sites.name: Apex Pass and the high ground west of Wolframite
sites.capacity: Open alpine ground at and around the pass with room for a small party or two on gravel and thin turf. No established sites, no facilities and no shelter of any kind from wind.
sites.water: Snowmelt and the odd tarn early in the season, and frequently nothing at all by late summer. This is a place you carry water to, not one you collect at. The last dependable source coming up is Tungsten Creek; coming from the Cathedral side it is the lake basins, which are a long way west. A party that has not carried enough will be walking a long way down for it.
sites.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit, no quota, no reservation anywhere in this wilderness. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass at whichever trailhead you used. Assume no fires — there is nothing to burn at this height and the alpine turf is fragile enough that a footprint lasts years, so pitch on gravel or rock.
sites.notes: The pass is where the Boundary Trail bends south a mile west of the Wolframite approach, and it is the link between this peak and the Cathedral country — Apex Mountain stands immediately above it, Amphitheater and Cathedral Peak are further west, and a party collecting summits along this crest will pass through here whichever direction they are travelling. As a camp it is bought and paid for in water and wind: the position is superb and the ground gives no protection at all. Its argument is position rather than comfort, since from here Wolframite is a short morning to the east and Apex is a short morning above. WHAT IT IS NOT is a substitute for a lower camp on a first night — a party arriving here tired and dry has made the trip harder, not easier. Snow lies on the north sides of these passes into late July in an ordinary year and much longer after a heavy winter, which is the real constraint on when the crest is worth traversing. Larches turn in the last days of September and the nights up here are properly cold by then.

sites.name: Teapot Lake and the Boundary Trail benches toward Bauerman Ridge
sites.capacity: Informal ground around the lake and on the benches either side of the trail, room for a party or two at each. Nothing developed, nothing signed, and long odds against meeting anyone.
sites.water: Teapot Lake is the dependable one on this stretch and that is precisely why parties camp at it rather than on the ridge — but it is a small standing body and has been found stagnant in a dry year, so treat it properly and take it from an inlet if there is one running. The streams and pools between here and the Wolframite junction go dry through the season and cannot be counted on.
sites.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit from whichever trailhead kiosk you started at, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Camp back from the shoreline. Weed-free feed for stock and no tying animals to trees overnight. Fires legal in existing rings outside a ban, but there is little to burn and the ground is thin.
sites.notes: The eastern half of the Wolframite corridor, and the camp for a party crossing between this peak and the Horseshoe Basin country rather than going in and out from the Chewuch. It is roughly fourteen miles of mild, high walking from the Tungsten junction east to Horseshoe Basin, staying largely above seven thousand feet, with Bauerman Ridge, Teapot Dome and Horseshoe Mountain all coming off the trail as short detours in the same way Wolframite does. THIS TRAVERSE IS DECIDED BY WATER AND NOT BY DISTANCE. In a dry September the crest carries almost nothing, and parties have walked it past empty pools and dry streambeds with this lake and the occasional trickle as the only supply — which turns a gentle high walk into a rationing exercise. Plan the days around the sources rather than around the miles, fill at every one, and treat any pool as suspect. The far end of this line is the Iron Gate trailhead above Toats Coulee, whose last six miles of road want high clearance, and whose Horseshoe Basin camps are recorded in the eastern Pasayten file rather than here.
